To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we describe two new cases of Matthew‐Wood Syndrome (MWS), a rare congenital malformation syndrome characterized by microphthalmia/anopthalmia, pulmonary aplasia, and diaphragm defect, and that we have performed a molecular study on the candidate genes FGF10 and FGF2 in these cases, and that we were not able to identify any causative mutations.
we have identified two new cases of Matthew‐Wood Syndrome, and we have excluded the genes FGF10 and FGF2 in these patients.

(1) we report the first cases of Matthew‐Wood Syndrome in consanguineus families, (2) we report the exclusion of FGF 10 and FGFR 2 as the cause for the syndrome in these families, (3) we propose that the FGF10/FGRF2 pathway is a candidate for MWS, and (4) we report that the phenotype in the sibs of one family is evocative of MWS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular genetic analysis of two new cases of Matthew‐Wood (MWS) syndrome.
the molecular genetic analysis of two families with a rare syndrome, known as Matthew‐ Wood syndrome (MWS).
the development of new methods for the analysis of the genetic structure of populations, and the use of these methods for the analysis and comparison of genetic structure of populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two cases described here represent a new example of Matthew‐Wood Syndrome.
the MWS gene is not located within the coding sequences of FGF10 or of FGFR2.
there is no evidence that the FGF10 or the FGFR2 gene are involved in the pathogenesis of the Matthew‐Wood syndrome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Matthew‐Wood syndrome is an extremely rare condition, and that it is probably caused by a mutation in a single gene that is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
we have identified two new cases of MWS, which we believe to be autosomal recessive, and we have excluded the involvement of FGF10 or its cognate receptor FGFR2 as the cause of MWS.

we have described two cases of Matthew‐Wood Syndrome in two unrelated consanguineous Turkish families, which is the first report from the Turkish population, and the third report of consanguineous cases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Matthew‐Wood syndrome can occur as a recessive trait, and that it can be transmitted from one sibling to the next, even if the intervening generation is phenotypically normal.
Matthew‐Wood syndrome is a rare, but recognizable, association of congenital anomalies that can be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
MWS should be added to the list of syndromes associated with pulmonary agenesis.
